title: The single life
hookLine: single people also live a calling of love and service

lines: A WEEK OF ONE SINGLE MAN.
cards: A question single people sometimes get at family weddings: so, when's it your turn? Asked kindly, over cake, as if life were a waiting room and the real thing starts at the altar. Meanwhile, look at one single man's week.
Tuesday, he drives his elderly neighbor to the cardiologist. Wednesday, he's the one his sister calls at midnight. Saturday, he coaches nine-year-olds who think he's the funniest man alive.
Sunday, he reads at the early Mass. Nobody at the wedding asked about any of that.

teach.h: THE GOSPELS GIVE JESUS NO WIFE.
teach.b: Start with something easy to skip: the Gospels give Jesus no wife. Neither, as far as his letters let us see, did Paul, and he writes about it to Corinth with real warmth.

teach.h: EVERY ONE HATH HIS PROPER GIFT.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "For I would that all men were even as myself: but every one hath his proper gift from God; one after this manner, and another after that." Notice the word gift.
Marriage is a gift; so is the unmarried life.

teach.h: ROOM FOR THE THINGS OF THE LORD.
teach.b: Then he says why it matters: "He that is without a wife, is solicitous for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please God."
The unmarried person, Paul says, has room: for prayer, for friends, for people who need someone to show up. The Catechism speaks to single people directly.
It says many live single not by their own choice, because of the circumstances of their lives, and that they are especially close to the heart of Jesus.

teach.h: THE CHURCH IS A HOME FOR EVERYONE.
teach.b: It asks parishes to open their doors to them, and says no one is without a family in this world: the Church is a home and family for everyone. So the Catholic picture isn't of a person waiting for a vocation to begin.

teach.h: EVERY ONE HATH HIS PROPER GIFT FROM GOD.
teach.b: The call to holiness from two days ago is already theirs, whole. Some single people take a vow later, some marry later, and some live single all their lives. None of those seasons is a gap in the calling.
Love and service don't need a ring to count. The neighbor at the cardiologist knows that.

how: Single Catholics live the call to holiness in their work, friendships, family and parish, without vows of religious life. The Catechism asks parishes to welcome single people and describes the Church as a home and family for everyone.

o: a waiting time before a person's real vocation
a life of vows lived alone, apart from others
an unmarried life that is already a whole calling

games.q: you're Paul, writing to a church in Corinth full of questions about marriage. some are married, some aren't. what do you tell the unmarried?
o: hurry up and marry; that's where holiness starts.
every one has his own gift from God, and the unmarried have room for the things of the Lord.
the unmarried should leave the church until they marry.
games.why: Paul calls each state a gift, and says the unmarried person is "solicitous for the things that belong to the Lord."

practice: Bring to mind someone you know who is single, a friend, an aunt, a widower down the street, or yourself, and one specific way they show up for people: the drive, the call, the meal.
If you pray, thank God for them by name, and ask that they be loved as they love. If you don't, let gratitude for them fill the sit.

wordCard.voice: The single life. In Catholic teaching, a life lived unmarried, by choice or by circumstance, that is already a whole calling to love and service. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, unmarried: Paul's word in 1 Corinthians 7 for the person with room for the things of the Lord.

carryVoice: Your line: a whole calling. No season of life is a waiting room. Same time tomorrow.
